questions.q: Opechancanough, the Powhatan leader who directed the 1622 and 1644 attacks on English Virginia, met what end in 1646?
options: He died of smallpox while bargaining for a peace treaty at Jamestown
He fled west and lived out his life among the Monacan
He was captured and later shot by a guard while held at Jamestown
He was shipped to England and died in the Tower of London
questions.explain: Captured by Governor William Berkeley's men, the aged leader was shot in the back by an English soldier while a prisoner at Jamestown.

questions.q: The 1646 treaty that ended the last Anglo-Powhatan War left the Powhatan peoples in what position?
options: Tributaries paying Virginia a yearly tribute of beaver skins
Equal partners sharing the Jamestown peninsula with English settlers
Subjects of the Spanish governor of Florida
questions.explain: Under the treaty, the Powhatan ceded land between the James and York rivers and paid a yearly tribute of beaver skins to Virginia's governor.

questions.q: Which Pamunkey leader signed the 1677 Treaty of Middle Plantation, which confirmed land rights for Native tributary towns in Virginia?
questions.explain: Cockacoeske, a female leader of the Pamunkey, signed the treaty after Bacon's Rebellion and was recognized as overlord of several tributary peoples.

questions.q: In September 1676, after Governor William Berkeley fled, what did Nathaniel Bacon's followers do to Jamestown?
options: Fortified it as the capital of a new colony
Burned the town, including its statehouse and church
Handed it to a Dutch fleet in the James River
Turned it over to the Susquehannock as ransom
questions.explain: Bacon's men burned Jamestown on September 19, 1676, so that Berkeley could not use it as a base; the capital later moved to Williamsburg.

questions.q: How did Nathaniel Bacon die in October 1676?
options: By hanging in Jamestown after a trial before Berkeley
Of dysentery and fever while his rebellion was still going on
In battle against the Occaneechi on the Roanoke River
Shot by royal soldiers who had just landed from England
questions.explain: Bacon died of the 'bloody flux' (dysentery) and fever; without him the uprising collapsed, and Berkeley hanged more than twenty rebels.

questions.q: In May 1676, Bacon's volunteers turned on which Native people, who had just helped them by attacking a Susquehannock camp?
questions.explain: After the Occaneechi defeated a Susquehannock band, Bacon's men quarreled with them over captives and plunder and attacked their island town.

questions.q: The three ships that brought the first Jamestown colonists in 1607 were the Godspeed, the Discovery and which larger flagship?
questions.explain: Captain Christopher Newport commanded the Susan Constant, the largest of the three ships that reached Virginia in the spring of 1607.

questions.q: The Sea Venture, flagship of a 1609 relief fleet bound for Jamestown, was wrecked on which island group?
questions.explain: The castaways built two small ships and reached Jamestown in 1610; their story is thought to have helped inspire Shakespeare's The Tempest.

questions.q: What was the harsh code of rules imposed on Jamestown in 1610-1611 under Thomas Gates and Thomas Dale?
options: The Laws Divine, Moral and Martial
questions.explain: The martial-law code punished offenses such as stealing food or skipping work with whipping or death, as the company tried to save the colony.

questions.q: In June 1610, Jamestown's starving survivors were sailing away when they met the arriving ships of which new governor?
questions.explain: De La Warr's fleet arrived with supplies and new settlers, and he ordered the colonists back to Jamestown just after the Starving Time.

questions.q: Which settlement, founded in 1634, served as Maryland's first capital?
questions.explain: Colonists from the Ark and the Dove founded St. Mary's City near the mouth of the Potomac; it remained the capital until the 1690s.

questions.q: Which Maryland rebel led the Protestant Association that overthrew the Calvert family's government in 1689?
questions.explain: Coode's Protestant Associators seized power after the Glorious Revolution, and the Crown soon took over Maryland as a royal colony.

questions.q: Which English soldier served as Plymouth Colony's military leader?
questions.explain: Standish, a professional soldier, led Plymouth's militia and in 1623 led a raid on Massachusett men at Wessagusset.

questions.q: Thomas Morton angered Plymouth's leaders at his Merrymount trading post in the 1620s chiefly by doing what?
options: Raising a maypole and selling guns to Native people
Claiming the land for the Dutch West India Company
Refusing to pay a tax levied by King Charles I
Printing pamphlets that mocked the Church of England
questions.explain: Plymouth's Myles Standish arrested Morton in 1628, and he was shipped back to England; Morton mocked the Puritans in his book New English Canaan.

questions.q: Under the 1629 Cambridge Agreement, Puritan leaders of the Massachusetts Bay Company decided to do what?
options: Ask the king to name a royal governor for their colony
Sell their shares to Dutch merchants in Leiden
Send only indentured servants to clear and settle the colony at first
Carry the company's charter and government with them to New England
questions.explain: Taking the charter to Massachusetts let the colony govern itself far from company shareholders and royal officials in London.

questions.q: John Winthrop sailed to Massachusetts Bay in 1630 aboard which flagship of the Puritan fleet?
questions.explain: The Arbella led the Winthrop Fleet of eleven ships; Winthrop's famous 'city upon a hill' sermon is traditionally linked to the voyage.

questions.q: Which New England colony was left out of the New England Confederation formed in 1643?
questions.explain: The United Colonies of New England joined Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth, Connecticut and New Haven for defense; Rhode Island's dissenters were excluded.

questions.q: Which Connecticut captain led the 1637 attack on the Pequot fort at Mystic?
questions.explain: Mason, with John Underhill and Mohegan and Narragansett allies, set the fort on fire; hundreds of Pequot, many of them women and children, were killed.

questions.q: Which Mohegan sachem allied with the English against the Pequot in 1637?
questions.explain: Uncas broke from the Pequot and sided with the English, making the Mohegan a leading power in southern New England after the war.

questions.q: In 1643 the United Colonies approved the execution of which Narragansett sachem, then a captive of the Mohegan leader Uncas?
questions.explain: Miantonomi was captured in battle with the Mohegan; with English approval, Uncas's brother killed him, deepening Narragansett anger at the colonists.

questions.q: The 1675 death of which Christian Native interpreter, and the hanging of three Wampanoag men for it, helped start King Philip's War?
questions.explain: Sassamon had warned Plymouth of Metacom's plans; Plymouth's trial and execution of three Wampanoag men for his death brought war that June.

questions.q: Metacom was killed in August 1676 by a Native soldier serving in the company of which colonial captain?
questions.explain: Church's mixed English and Native company tracked Metacom to Mount Hope, where a Native man named John Alderman shot him.

questions.q: Which enslaved woman in minister Samuel Parris's household was among the first people accused of witchcraft in Salem in 1692?
questions.explain: Tituba confessed under pressure and described a conspiracy of witches, which fed the panic; she was jailed but not executed.

questions.q: Governor William Phips created which special court to hear the Salem witchcraft cases in 1692?
options: The Court of Oyer and Terminer
questions.explain: The court, led by William Stoughton, condemned the accused; Phips dissolved it in October 1692 as doubts about spectral evidence grew.

questions.q: Which Salem judge stood in Boston's Old South Meeting House in 1697 while a statement taking the blame for his role was read?
questions.explain: Sewall was the only judge to publicly apologize; Stoughton and Hathorne never did.

questions.q: Which Baptist minister secured Rhode Island's 1663 royal charter, with its promise of a 'lively experiment' in religious liberty?
questions.explain: Clarke spent years in London lobbying for the charter, which guaranteed that no one would be punished for differences in religious opinion.

questions.q: Fort Christina, the main settlement of New Sweden founded in 1638, stood at the site of which present-day city?
questions.explain: Peter Minuit led the Swedish expedition, naming the fort for Sweden's young Queen Christina.

questions.q: Which governor led the Dutch takeover of New Sweden in 1655?
questions.explain: Stuyvesant sailed up the Delaware with several hundred soldiers, and the Swedish colony surrendered without a major battle.

questions.q: Willem Kieft, director of New Netherland, set off a 1643-1645 war after soldiers massacred Native refugees at which place?
questions.explain: The February 1643 killings at Pavonia, across the Hudson from Manhattan, provoked Lenape attacks that nearly destroyed the colony's outlying farms.

questions.q: The Duke of York granted New Jersey in 1664 to which two proprietors?
options: Anthony Ashley Cooper and John Locke
questions.explain: Carteret had defended the island of Jersey for the Crown during England's civil war, giving the colony its name.

questions.q: What did William Penn call his plan for a colony founded on Quaker principles?
questions.explain: Penn hoped Pennsylvania would show that a government could rest on religious liberty, peace and fair dealing.

questions.q: What happened to Jacob Leisler after his rebellion in New York ended in 1691?
options: He became the colony's royal governor
He fled to the Dutch colony at Curacao
He was convicted of treason and hanged
He was pardoned and elected to the assembly
questions.explain: Leisler and his son-in-law Jacob Milborne were executed in May 1691; Parliament reversed their attainders in 1695.

questions.q: In 1719, South Carolina colonists overthrew whose rule after the Yamasee War exposed weak defenses?
questions.explain: Colonists asked the Crown to take over; South Carolina came under royal government, and the Crown bought out the proprietors in 1729.

questions.q: Which surveyor, author of A New Voyage to Carolina, was executed by the Tuscarora in 1711?
questions.explain: Lawson and Graffenried were captured on a trip up the Neuse River; Graffenried was released, but Lawson was killed as the war began.

questions.q: What turned the Yamasee War in South Carolina's favor in early 1716?
options: A Spanish fleet arrived to defend Charles Town
The Cherokee sided with the colony against the Creek
The Yamasee surrendered after a smallpox outbreak
Virginia sent an army of several thousand men
questions.explain: After Cherokee leaders killed Creek envoys at Tugaloo, the Cherokee joined South Carolina, and the Creek and their allies pulled back.

questions.q: Which Yamacraw leader welcomed James Oglethorpe and helped Georgia's founders at Savannah in 1733?
questions.explain: Tomochichi granted land for Savannah and traveled to London in 1734, where he met King George II.

questions.q: Which Creek-English woman served as James Oglethorpe's interpreter and trade go-between in early Georgia?
questions.explain: Mary Musgrove (Coosaponakeesa) ran a trading post near Savannah and helped Georgia keep peace with the Creek.

questions.q: The War of Jenkins' Ear, which began between Britain and Spain in 1739, was named for what?
options: A British captain's ear, cut off by a Spanish coast guard officer
A Spanish governor's ear lost in a sword duel with James Oglethorpe
A Georgia trader's ear cut off by Creek warriors
A sailor's ear lost in a mutiny aboard a slave ship
questions.explain: Robert Jenkins said Spanish coast guards boarded his ship in 1731 and cut off his ear; he displayed it to Parliament years later.

questions.q: Which Tewa religious leader organized the Pueblo Revolt of 1680?
questions.explain: Popé directed the revolt from Taos; a marble statue of him represents New Mexico in the U.S. Capitol's National Statuary Hall collection.

questions.q: Which Spanish governor led the reconquest of New Mexico beginning in 1692?
questions.explain: Otermin was the governor who fled in 1680; Vargas returned twelve years later and reoccupied Santa Fe by 1693.

questions.q: How did Pueblo runners coordinate the start of the 1680 revolt across many towns?
options: By sending painted shields to each town's leaders
By carrying knotted cords, with one knot untied each day
By lighting signal fires on a chain of mesas
By passing letters written in Spanish by mission scribes
questions.explain: When the last knot was untied, the towns were to rise together; the revolt began on August 10, 1680.

questions.q: Which Jesuit missionary founded missions in the Pimeria Alta, in present-day Sonora and Arizona, beginning in 1687?
questions.explain: Kino founded more than twenty missions, including San Xavier del Bac near Tucson, and mapped the region.

questions.q: La Salle's 1685 colony, which alarmed Spain, was planted by mistake on the coast of which present-day state?
questions.explain: Aiming for the mouth of the Mississippi, La Salle landed at Matagorda Bay; he was killed by his own men in 1687.

questions.q: The Jesuit Relations, published yearly from 1632 to 1673, were what?
options: Treaties signed between New France and the Haudenosaunee nations
Royal laws governing the fur trade
Missionaries' reports from New France printed in France
Letters from Huguenot settlers in Carolina
questions.explain: The reports described Native peoples and mission work in detail and are a major source for the history of New France.

questions.q: In 1649, Haudenosaunee attacks destroyed the homeland and Jesuit missions of which Iroquoian-speaking confederacy?
questions.explain: Weakened by epidemics, the Wendat were scattered by Haudenosaunee raids; survivors moved near Quebec or west to the Great Lakes.

questions.q: In 1673, missionary Jacques Marquette and which fur trader traveled down the Mississippi River as far as the Arkansas River?
questions.explain: Jolliet and Marquette turned back near the Arkansas after learning the river flowed to the Gulf of Mexico, not the Pacific.

questions.q: Which French Canadian brothers led the founding of Louisiana, including Mobile and New Orleans?
questions.explain: Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville founded the first posts in 1699; his brother Jean-Baptiste, sieur de Bienville, founded New Orleans in 1718.

questions.q: John Law's company, which promoted French Louisiana, collapsed in 1720 in a speculative crash known as what?
questions.explain: Law's Mississippi Company sold shares on promises of Louisiana riches; when the bubble burst, French investors were ruined.

questions.q: At the 1744 Treaty of Lancaster, which Onondaga speaker urged the colonies to unite as the Haudenosaunee nations had?
questions.explain: Benjamin Franklin printed the treaty proceedings, and Canasatego's advice is often cited in discussions of the Albany Plan.

questions.q: England's Navigation Act of 1651 was aimed mainly at the shipping trade of which rival?
questions.explain: Dutch merchants dominated colonial carrying trade; the act helped bring on the First Anglo-Dutch War in 1652.

questions.q: Which formerly enslaved man commanded the Black militia at Fort Mose in Spanish Florida?
questions.explain: Menendez, who had escaped slavery in Carolina, led the free Black militia that helped defeat Oglethorpe's forces at Fort Mose in 1740.

questions.q: The 1741 conspiracy trials in New York City relied heavily on the testimony of which indentured servant?
questions.explain: Burton, a servant at John Hughson's tavern, named many alleged plotters; dozens of enslaved men were burned or hanged.

questions.q: In 1640, a Virginia court sentenced John Punch, a runaway servant of African descent, to what?
options: Return to Africa on the next ship
Serve his master for the rest of his life
Pay a fine in tobacco and go free
Join the colony's militia for seven years
questions.explain: The two European servants who ran with Punch received only extra years, so his case is often cited as the first legal record of lifelong slavery in Virginia.

questions.q: Most indentured servants bound for the Chesapeake in the 1600s signed contracts for about how long?
questions.explain: Terms usually ran four to seven years, and younger servants without contracts often served longer under local custom.

questions.q: Jonathan Edwards described the 1734-1735 revival in his Northampton church in which widely read work?
options: A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God
The Danger of an Unconverted Ministry
questions.explain: Published in 1737, the Faithful Narrative was read in Britain and the colonies and became a model account of revival.

questions.q: In 1750, Northampton's congregation dismissed Jonathan Edwards mainly over what?
options: His public support for the Old Lights
His refusal to preach at outdoor revivals
His stricter rules for admitting people to communion
His plan to merge with the Church of England
questions.explain: Edwards insisted that communicants show evidence of conversion, reversing his grandfather Solomon Stoddard's open practice.

questions.q: Which Boston minister was the leading Old Light critic of the revivals of the 1740s?
questions.explain: Chauncy's Seasonable Thoughts on the State of Religion (1743) attacked the revivals' emotional excesses.

questions.q: George Whitefield raised money across the colonies for which institution in Georgia?
questions.explain: Whitefield founded the Bethesda Orphan House in 1740 and collected gifts for it on his preaching tours.

questions.q: Which English founder of the Society of Friends toured the American colonies in 1671-1673?
questions.explain: Fox visited Quaker meetings from Barbados and Maryland to Rhode Island, strengthening the young Quaker communities.

questions.q: Quaker John Woolman's 1754 essay Some Considerations on the Keeping of Negroes urged what?
options: That Friends give up holding people in slavery
That Quakers move to the frontier to convert Native peoples
That Pennsylvania ban all imports from Britain
That Friends stop paying taxes for war
questions.explain: Woolman traveled among Quaker meetings urging members to free enslaved people; Philadelphia Friends moved against slaveholding in 1758 and after.

questions.q: Parliament shut down the Massachusetts Land Bank in 1741 by extending which law to the colonies?
questions.explain: The Land Bank issued notes backed by mortgages; its closure ruined many investors, including Samuel Adams's father.

questions.q: After the statehouse at Jamestown burned in 1698, Virginia moved its capital to which town?
questions.explain: The new capital grew from Middle Plantation and was renamed for King William III; Richmond became the capital in 1780.

questions.q: In 1728, Virginia planter William Byrd II led a survey to fix the boundary between Virginia and which colony?
questions.explain: Byrd's witty History of the Dividing Line describes the survey through the Great Dismal Swamp.

questions.q: Which Boston minister went to London and helped negotiate Massachusetts's new charter of 1691?
questions.explain: Increase Mather could not restore the old charter but won a new one and helped choose William Phips as governor.

questions.q: According to Connecticut legend, colonists hid their charter from Edmund Andros in 1687 in what place?
questions.explain: The tree, later called the Charter Oak, stood in Hartford until a storm toppled it in 1856.

questions.q: In February 1690, during King William's War, French and Native forces destroyed which New York frontier village?
questions.explain: The night raid killed about sixty people and alarmed the English colonies, which planned a failed attack on Quebec that year.

questions.q: The 1704 French and Native raid on Deerfield, Massachusetts, took place during which war?
questions.explain: Raiders killed dozens of residents and marched more than one hundred captives to Canada, including minister John Williams.

questions.q: Which Maine merchant commanded the New England army in the 1745 siege of France's fortress on Cape Breton Island?
questions.explain: Governor William Shirley organized the expedition against Louisbourg; Pepperrell led the troops and was made a baronet after its capture.

questions.q: Pocahontas died in 1617 at the start of a voyage home and was buried in which English town?
questions.explain: She fell ill as her ship set out down the Thames and was buried at St George's Church in Gravesend.

questions.q: Which Abenaki sachem startled the Plymouth settlers in March 1621 by walking into their settlement and greeting them in English?
questions.explain: Samoset had learned some English from fishermen in Maine; he soon returned with Tisquantum (Squanto), who spoke English better.

questions.q: Founded in 1635, which is the oldest public school in the United States?
questions.explain: Boston's town meeting voted to support a schoolmaster in 1635; Boston Latin's students later included Benjamin Franklin, who did not graduate.

questions.q: Which learned society did Benjamin Franklin help found in Philadelphia in 1743?
options: The American Academy of Arts and Sciences
questions.explain: Franklin proposed a society to share 'useful knowledge' among colonial scientists; it still meets in Philadelphia.

questions.q: In 1751, Benjamin Franklin and physician Thomas Bond founded which Philadelphia institution?
questions.explain: Pennsylvania Hospital cared for the sick poor and the mentally ill; Franklin raised matching funds from the assembly.

questions.q: Franklin's 1742 'Pennsylvania fireplace,' later called the Franklin stove, was designed to do what?
options: Heat a room better while burning less wood
Cook food without any open flame
Smelt iron ore for colonial forges
Light city streets with burning oil
questions.explain: Franklin refused a patent, saying people should share in inventions freely as they benefited from others'.

questions.q: Boston merchant Peter Faneuil gave the town what building in 1742?
options: A Huguenot church and burial ground
A lighthouse at the harbor's entrance
A grammar school for poor boys
A market hall with a meeting room above it
questions.explain: Faneuil Hall later hosted protest meetings in the 1760s and 1770s; part of Faneuil's fortune came from trade tied to slavery.

questions.q: Alexander Spotswood's 1716 expedition, whose members became known as the Knights of the Golden Horseshoe, crossed the Blue Ridge into which valley?
questions.explain: Spotswood promoted settlement west of the Blue Ridge; according to tradition, he gave members small golden horseshoes to mark the journey.

questions.q: In 1752, French-allied warriors led by Charles Langlade destroyed Pickawillany, a trading town of which people?
questions.explain: The Miami leader Memeskia, called Old Briton for his British trade ties, was killed, warning British traders off the Ohio country.

questions.q: Harvard's first president, Henry Dunster, was forced to resign in 1654 for rejecting what practice?
questions.explain: Dunster's Baptist views clashed with Massachusetts law, which required infant baptism.

questions.q: The 1811 German Coast Uprising, the largest slave revolt in U.S. history, took place in which territory?
questions.explain: Hundreds of enslaved people marched toward New Orleans along the Mississippi before militia and federal troops crushed the revolt.

questions.q: Denmark Vesey, executed in 1822 for planning a revolt in Charleston, had earlier bought his freedom with what?
options: Wages from service in the War of 1812
Gold found on the Georgia frontier
Prize money from a city lottery
A loan from the American Colonization Society
questions.explain: Vesey won $1,500 in a 1799 lottery and bought his freedom; Charleston later destroyed the AME church where he worshiped.

questions.q: South Carolina's Negro Seamen Act of 1822 required what?
options: Paying Black sailors the same wages as white sailors
Banning Black sailors from the U.S. Navy
Freeing any enslaved person who reached a ship
Jailing free Black sailors while their ships stayed in port
questions.explain: Passed after the Vesey plot, the law angered Britain; a federal judge called it unconstitutional, but South Carolina kept enforcing it.

questions.q: Nat Turner took which natural event in February 1831 as a sign to prepare his revolt?
questions.explain: Turner saw the eclipse as a divine signal; the revolt began that August in Southampton County, Virginia.

questions.q: In Barron v. Baltimore (1833), Chief Justice Marshall's Court held what?
options: States could not tax a bank chartered by Congress
The Bill of Rights limited only the federal government, not the states
Cities had no power to regulate their harbors
Private property could never be taken for public use, even with payment
questions.explain: A wharf owner claimed the city had taken his property without compensation; the Fourteenth Amendment later opened the way to applying rights to the states.

questions.q: In Johnson v. M'Intosh (1823), the Supreme Court ruled what about Native land?
options: Only the federal government could acquire it from Native nations
Native nations could sell it to any private buyer
States owned all of it within their borders
Settlers gained title after living on it for seven years
questions.explain: Marshall's opinion relied on the 'doctrine of discovery,' holding that private purchases from tribes gave no valid title.

questions.q: Who succeeded John Marshall as chief justice of the United States in 1836?
questions.explain: Taney, Jackson's former Treasury secretary, led the Court until 1864; he is best known for the Dred Scott decision.

questions.q: Prigg v. Pennsylvania (1842) struck down a Pennsylvania law because it conflicted with what?
options: The federal Fugitive Slave Act of 1793
questions.explain: The Court also said states need not help enforce the federal law, which led several northern states to pass personal liberty laws.

questions.q: Which Treasury secretary under Jefferson and Madison worked to pay down the national debt and wrote an 1808 report on roads and canals?
questions.explain: Gallatin, born in Geneva, served from 1801 to 1814, the longest of any Treasury secretary, and later helped negotiate the Treaty of Ghent.

questions.q: Which U.S. Army general, secretly a paid Spanish agent, exposed Aaron Burr's western scheme to Jefferson?
questions.explain: Wilkinson had conspired with Burr before turning on him; his secret Spanish pension was confirmed by documents found after his death.

questions.q: Who became the first governor of the Territory of Orleans, the southern part of the Louisiana Purchase?
questions.explain: Claiborne received Louisiana from France in December 1803 and later became the first governor of the state of Louisiana.

questions.q: In 1804, Stephen Decatur led a daring night raid into a Barbary Coast harbor to do what?
options: Blow up the city's main fort
Burn the captured U.S. frigate Philadelphia
questions.explain: Decatur's men slipped in on a captured ketch and set the Philadelphia ablaze; Britain's Admiral Nelson reportedly praised the raid.

questions.q: The USS Constitution earned the nickname 'Old Ironsides' in an 1812 victory over which British frigate?
questions.explain: Sailors said British cannonballs bounced off the Constitution's thick oak sides, and the frigate won again against HMS Java that December.

questions.q: Which U.S. commander reported 'We have met the enemy and they are ours' after a battle on Lake Erie in 1813?
questions.explain: Perry's victory gave the United States control of Lake Erie and forced the British to give up Detroit.

questions.q: Tecumseh was killed in October 1813 at which battle in Upper Canada?
questions.explain: William Henry Harrison's army defeated the British and their Native allies; Tecumseh's death broke up his confederacy.

questions.q: In 1813, American troops burned public buildings at York, the capital of Upper Canada. York is now which city?
questions.explain: The burning of York's parliament buildings was cited by the British as one reason for burning Washington in 1814.

questions.q: Thomas Macdonough's September 1814 naval victory stopped a British invasion from Canada on which lake?
questions.explain: The Battle of Plattsburgh forced British troops back to Canada and strengthened the U.S. position at the Ghent peace talks.

questions.q: The August 1813 Red Stick attack on which Alabama stockade drew the United States into the Creek War?
questions.explain: Red Stick warriors killed hundreds of settlers, militia and enslaved people at Fort Mims north of Mobile.

questions.q: Which Barataria Bay privateer and his men helped Andrew Jackson defend New Orleans in 1814-1815?
questions.explain: Lafitte turned down a British offer and provided men, flints and powder; Madison later pardoned the Baratarians.

questions.q: After the British burned the White House, President Madison signed the ratified Treaty of Ghent in 1815 in which nearby house?
questions.explain: The Madisons lived in the Octagon, owned by John Tayloe III, while the White House was rebuilt; the treaty was signed in its upstairs study.

questions.q: In the 1820 election, James Monroe won every electoral vote but one. Who received that lone vote?
questions.explain: New Hampshire elector William Plumer voted for Adams, Monroe's secretary of state, reportedly because he thought Monroe a weak leader.

questions.q: British foreign secretary George Canning proposed in 1823 that the United States and Britain do what?
options: Divide the Oregon Country between them at the line of the Columbia River
Jointly warn other European powers against intervening in Latin America
End the Atlantic slave trade by naval patrols
questions.explain: John Quincy Adams persuaded Monroe to act alone, and the United States issued the Monroe Doctrine that December.

questions.q: Besides Jackson, John Quincy Adams and Henry Clay, who was the fourth major presidential candidate in 1824, a Georgian slowed by a stroke?
questions.explain: Crawford, Monroe's Treasury secretary, finished third in electoral votes, ahead of Clay, so Clay could not be considered by the House.

questions.q: Andrew Jackson's 1830 Maysville Road veto rejected federal money for a road lying entirely within which state?
questions.explain: Jackson argued a purely local road was not a proper federal project; it was also a jab at Kentucky's Henry Clay.

questions.q: Which third party held the first national presidential nominating convention, in 1831?
questions.explain: Meeting in Baltimore, the Anti-Masons nominated William Wirt; the major parties soon adopted conventions too.

questions.q: In January 1835, the first known attempt to kill a sitting president failed outside the Capitol. Why?
options: A guard knocked the gun away just in time
The bullet struck a book in Jackson's coat
Both of the attacker's pistols misfired
The gunman lost his nerve and ran away
questions.explain: Richard Lawrence's two pistols misfired; Jackson went after him with his cane, and Lawrence was later found insane.

questions.q: Which Treasury secretary did Jackson fire in 1833 for refusing to remove federal deposits from the Second Bank?
questions.explain: Duane lasted only a few months; Jackson replaced him with Roger B. Taney, who moved the deposits to state banks.

questions.q: Critics mocked the first vice president to take over after a president's death with what nickname?
questions.explain: When Harrison died in 1841, John Tyler insisted he was fully president, not acting president, setting a lasting precedent.

questions.q: The Dorr Rebellion of 1841-1842 sought to do what in Rhode Island?
options: Extend voting rights to men without land
questions.explain: Rhode Island still used its 1663 charter, which limited voting to landowners; a new 1843 constitution widened suffrage.

questions.q: Who commanded the Texan defenders of the Alamo in 1836?
questions.explain: Travis, who shared command with Jim Bowie until Bowie fell ill, wrote a famous letter pledging 'victory or death.'

questions.q: After his capture at San Jacinto, Santa Anna signed which agreements accepting Texas independence?
questions.explain: Mexico's government refused to ratify the treaties, which Santa Anna signed as a prisoner.

questions.q: Which Tejano officer led a company of Tejano soldiers at the Battle of San Jacinto?
questions.explain: Seguin had left the Alamo as a messenger before it fell; he later became mayor of San Antonio.

questions.q: The Donner Party was trapped by snow in 1846-1847 in which mountain range?
questions.explain: Delayed by the untested Hastings Cutoff, the emigrants were stranded near Truckee Lake; about half died.

questions.q: In 1834 and 1836, Lowell mill women staged 'turnouts' to protest what?
options: A ban on attending church on Sundays
Wage cuts and higher boardinghouse charges
The hiring of Irish immigrant men
The closing of the company library
questions.explain: The 1834 strike failed and the 1836 strike won only partial rollbacks, but they showed that the young women saw themselves as 'daughters of freemen' with rights.

questions.q: The 'Rhode Island system' of textile labor, unlike the Lowell system, typically hired what?
options: Enslaved workers hired from the South
questions.explain: Mills in the Samuel Slater tradition built villages and hired families, with children doing much of the work.

questions.q: A November 1825 ceremony in which a keg of Lake Erie water was poured into New York Harbor was nicknamed what?
questions.explain: The ceremony marked the Erie Canal's opening; Governor DeWitt Clinton rode the boat Seneca Chief from Buffalo to New York City.

questions.q: About how long was the original Erie Canal when it opened in 1825?
questions.explain: The canal used 83 locks to climb more than 500 feet between the Hudson and Lake Erie, and it cut freight costs sharply.

questions.q: The term 'wildcat banks' in the 1830s referred to what?
options: Branches of the Second Bank of the United States opened in frontier towns and mining camps
Banks owned by fur trading companies
Loosely regulated state banks that issued more notes than they could redeem
Federal offices that sold public land
questions.explain: The name was said to come from banks set up in remote places where few could reach them to redeem notes.

questions.q: Samuel Colt patented what invention in the United States in 1836?
questions.explain: Colt's early company failed, but the Mexican-American War and Texas Rangers' orders later made his revolvers a success.

questions.q: Which minister's 1825 Six Sermons on Intemperance helped launch the temperance crusade?
questions.explain: Beecher, father of Harriet Beecher Stowe, called for total abstinence; the American Temperance Society formed in 1826.

questions.q: Under the Auburn system of prison discipline in New York, inmates did what?
options: Lived alone in solitary cells day and night and never left them
Worked together by day in silence and slept in separate cells
Earned early release by joining the army
Were hired out to farms during harvest
questions.explain: The Auburn model, cheaper than full solitary confinement, spread to most American prisons.

questions.q: Eastern State Penitentiary in Philadelphia, opened in 1829, became famous for what practice?
options: Keeping each prisoner alone in a cell
Letting prisoners run their own courts
questions.explain: Its 'separate system' was meant to bring penitence through solitude; Charles Dickens criticized it after a visit in 1842.

questions.q: Dorothea Dix's 1843 memorial described mentally ill people kept in cages, cellars and stalls in which state?
questions.explain: Dix's report to the Massachusetts legislature led to the expansion of the state hospital at Worcester.

questions.q: William Holmes McGuffey is known for what?
options: A series of graded school readers
questions.explain: First published in 1836, McGuffey Readers taught reading along with moral lessons and sold well over 100 million copies.

questions.q: Mary Lyon founded which women's seminary in Massachusetts in 1837?
questions.explain: Mount Holyoke Female Seminary kept costs low so that women of modest means could attend.

questions.q: Which Ohio college, founded in 1833, was among the first to admit both women and Black students?
questions.explain: Oberlin admitted Black students from 1835 and in 1841 granted bachelor's degrees to women.

questions.q: Prudence Crandall was arrested in 1833 for running what in Canterbury, Connecticut?
options: A station on the Underground Railroad
A printing press for abolitionist tracts
questions.explain: Connecticut passed a 'Black Law' to close her school, and a mob attacked the building in 1834.

questions.q: The 1834 Lane Seminary debates in Cincinnati, led by student Theodore Dwight Weld, were mainly about what?
questions.explain: After trustees banned the antislavery society, many students left for Oberlin, which became an abolitionist center.

questions.q: Before founding The Liberator, William Lloyd Garrison worked in Baltimore with which Quaker antislavery editor?
questions.explain: Garrison co-edited Lundy's Genius of Universal Emancipation and was jailed for libel against a slave-trading merchant.

questions.q: Which wealthy New York merchant brothers helped finance the American Anti-Slavery Society?
questions.explain: The evangelical Tappans also backed Oberlin College and the legal defense of the Amistad captives.

questions.q: In July 1835, a mob in Charleston, South Carolina, broke into the post office and burned what?
options: Abolitionist pamphlets mailed from the North
questions.explain: The American Anti-Slavery Society's postal campaign led southern postmasters to stop delivering abolitionist mail.

questions.q: Pennsylvania Hall, a meeting hall built by abolitionists in Philadelphia, met what fate in May 1838?
options: Congress seized it for a federal mint
It was sold to a slave trader
A mob burned it days after it opened
It became the state's first Black college
questions.explain: Rioters set the hall on fire during a women's antislavery convention, while firefighters protected only nearby buildings.

questions.q: Henry Highland Garnet's 1843 'Address to the Slaves' in Buffalo urged what?
options: That free Black Americans move to Liberia
That enslaved people resist their enslavers
That the North secede from the Union
questions.explain: A convention of Black leaders narrowly declined to endorse it; Frederick Douglass was among those who opposed it then.

questions.q: Which wealthy Black sailmaker in Philadelphia helped fund The Liberator in its early years?
questions.explain: Forten, a Revolutionary War veteran, opposed colonization and supported Garrison's paper.

questions.q: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott met in 1840 at which event, where women delegates were refused seats?
options: The founding of the Liberty Party in Albany
The Lane Seminary debates in Cincinnati
The World Anti-Slavery Convention in London
questions.explain: Angered by the exclusion, the two talked of holding a women's rights meeting, which they did at Seneca Falls in 1848.

questions.q: The 1848 Seneca Falls Convention met in which building?
questions.explain: The chapel belonged to antislavery Wesleyan Methodists; it later became part of Women's Rights National Historical Park.

questions.q: Which bishop built American Methodism's system of circuit-riding preachers?
questions.explain: Asbury rode an estimated quarter-million miles; Methodism became the largest American denomination by the mid-1800s.

questions.q: Followers of William Miller called October 22, 1844, the day the expected Second Coming did not occur, what?
questions.explain: Some Millerites later formed the Seventh-day Adventist Church.

questions.q: In 1839, Mormons founded which Illinois city, for a time one of the largest in the state?
questions.explain: After Joseph Smith's murder in 1844, Brigham Young led most residents out of Nauvoo toward Utah starting in 1846.

questions.q: Which Welsh industrialist bought New Harmony, Indiana, in 1825 for a socialist community?
questions.explain: Owen bought the town from George Rapp's Harmony Society; the experiment fell apart within about two years.

questions.q: Sabbatarian reformers in the late 1820s petitioned Congress to do what?
options: Stop the Post Office from moving mail on Sundays
questions.explain: Senator Richard M. Johnson's 1829 report rejected the petitions as mixing church and state.

questions.q: The Cherokee Phoenix, first published in 1828, was notable as what?
options: A treaty signed with the state of Georgia
The first newspaper published by a Native nation
A ship that carried Cherokee to Indian Territory
questions.explain: Edited by Elias Boudinot, it printed columns in English and in Sequoyah's Cherokee syllabary.

questions.q: In 1839, Major Ridge, John Ridge and Elias Boudinot were killed by fellow Cherokee in Indian Territory. Why?
options: They had sold Cherokee land to Texas
They had sided with the Seminole in war
They had tried to overthrow Principal Chief John Ross by force of arms
They had signed the removal treaty without the nation's consent
questions.explain: Cherokee law made selling national land without consent a capital crime, and Ridge himself had helped write that law.

questions.q: Which U.S. general commanded the troops who rounded up the Cherokee for removal in 1838?
questions.explain: Scott's soldiers forced Cherokee families into stockades; the nation then went west in detachments largely under Cherokee leadership.

questions.q: Seminole leader Osceola was seized in 1837 in what way?
options: In a night raid on his Everglades camp
While meeting under a white flag of truce
After a Seminole rival betrayed him in Cuba
When his ship was stopped off the Florida Keys
questions.explain: General Thomas Jesup's capture of Osceola under a flag of truce drew widespread criticism; Osceola died in prison in 1838.

questions.q: Black Hawk, whose band's 1832 return across the Mississippi set off the Black Hawk War, was a leader of which people?
questions.explain: Black Hawk led a band of Sauk and Meskwaki back across the Mississippi to reclaim their village lands; his autobiography was published in 1833.

questions.q: In the 1832 Treaty of Pontotoc Creek, which nation agreed to sell its Mississippi homeland?
questions.explain: The Chickasaw moved west in the late 1830s, settling among the Choctaw in Indian Territory.

questions.q: Which New Jersey senator spoke for about six hours over three days against the Indian Removal Act in 1830?
questions.explain: Frelinghuysen, called the 'Christian statesman,' argued removal broke treaties; he was Clay's running mate in 1844.

questions.q: Which writer created the stories 'Rip Van Winkle' and 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow'?
questions.explain: Both stories appeared in The Sketch Book (1819-1820), which made Irving the first American author famous in Europe.

questions.q: James Smithson, whose bequest led Congress to create the Smithsonian Institution in 1846, was a scientist from which country?
questions.explain: Smithson never visited the United States; his gold sovereigns arrived in 1838, and Congress debated for years how to use them.

questions.q: After the Treasury building burned in 1833, which architect designed its replacement?
questions.explain: Mills's Greek Revival design, begun in 1836, forms the oldest wing of the Treasury Building beside the White House.

questions.q: Which Boston architect completed the U.S. Capitol and its first low wooden dome in the 1820s?
questions.explain: Bulfinch succeeded Latrobe in 1818; his copper-covered dome was replaced by Walter's cast-iron dome in the 1850s and 1860s.

questions.q: The 1809 Treaty of Fort Wayne angered Tecumseh because it did what?
options: Ceded about 3 million acres of Native land in Indiana Territory
Moved the Shawnee and Lenape to new lands west of the Mississippi River
Banned Native peoples from trading with Britain
questions.explain: Tecumseh argued that no single nation could sell land that belonged to all Native peoples in common.

questions.q: John Horse (Juan Caballo) was a leader of which group during the Second Seminole War?
questions.explain: Black Seminoles, many descended from people who escaped slavery, fought beside the Seminole; John Horse later led a group to Mexico.

questions.q: In 1837, who became the only vice president ever chosen by the Senate, after no candidate won an electoral majority?
questions.explain: Virginia's electors refused to vote for Johnson, so the Senate chose between him and Whig Francis Granger under the Twelfth Amendment.

questions.q: Robert Fulton's Clermont made its famous 1807 voyage up the Hudson River from New York City to which town?
questions.explain: The roughly 150-mile trip took about 32 hours, far faster than a sloop against the current.

questions.q: In 1787, John Fitch demonstrated an early steamboat for delegates to the Constitutional Convention on which river?
questions.explain: Fitch later ran a short-lived passenger service near Philadelphia, nearly two decades before Fulton's commercial success.

questions.q: The Comstock Lode, discovered in 1859 in present-day Nevada, was a huge deposit of which metal?
questions.explain: The strike built Virginia City and helped Nevada gain statehood in 1864.

questions.q: The Pony Express of 1860-1861 carried mail by relays of horseback riders between Missouri and which state?
questions.explain: Riders cut mail time to about ten days; the service ended when the transcontinental telegraph was finished in October 1861.

questions.q: The giant Corliss steam engine powered Machinery Hall at which 1876 event?
options: The World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago
The opening of the Brooklyn Bridge
questions.explain: President Grant and Brazil's Emperor Pedro II started the engine, which drove machines throughout the hall.

questions.q: Completed in 1874, James B. Eads's bridge across the Mississippi at St. Louis was the first major bridge to use what material?
questions.explain: Eads used steel arches and deep caissons sunk to bedrock; the bridge still carries traffic and light rail.

questions.q: Milwaukee printer Christopher Latham Sholes helped invent which machine, patented in 1868?
questions.explain: Sholes's design, sold to Remington, introduced the QWERTY keyboard layout.

questions.q: Thomas Edison's Pearl Street Station, opened in 1882, supplied electric power to customers in which city?
questions.explain: The coal-fired plant in lower Manhattan was the first commercial central power station in the United States, serving dozens of customers at first.

questions.q: Which soil scientist led the Soil Conservation Service created in 1935?
questions.explain: Bennett, called the father of soil conservation, reportedly timed testimony to Congress as a dust storm darkened Washington.

questions.q: The Tennessee Valley Authority's first dam, completed in 1936, was named for which senator?
questions.explain: Norris of Nebraska had pushed for public power at Muscle Shoals for years before the TVA was created in 1933.

questions.q: In January 1919, a huge storage tank burst in Boston's North End, sending a wave of what through the streets?
questions.explain: The Great Molasses Flood killed 21 people; the tank's owner was found responsible for building it poorly.

questions.q: After a hurricane killed thousands in 1900, which Texas city pioneered the city commission form of government?
questions.explain: The storm was the deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history; Galveston also raised its ground level and built a seawall.

questions.q: Promoted beginning in 1913, the Lincoln Highway was the first what?
options: Paved road in the national parks
Road across the United States from coast to coast
Toll road built by a railroad
questions.explain: The route ran from New York City to San Francisco and was backed by auto and tire makers such as Carl Fisher.

questions.q: The Colorado River Compact of 1922, negotiated with Commerce Secretary Herbert Hoover's help, divided the river's water how?
options: Equally between the United States and Mexico
Between an Upper Basin and a Lower Basin group of states
Among Native nations along the river
Between farms and cities by a fixed formula
questions.explain: Seven states signed the compact, which set the stage for Hoover Dam; Mexico's share was settled by a 1944 treaty.

questions.q: Great Smoky Mountains National Park, established in 1934, lies on the border of which two states?
questions.explain: Unlike western parks carved from federal land, it was assembled from private land bought with state funds and a large Rockefeller gift.

questions.q: In the early 1920s, Henry Ford offered to buy or lease which unfinished federal dam and nitrate plants on the Tennessee River?
questions.explain: Senator George Norris blocked the sale and pushed for public ownership, which led to the Tennessee Valley Authority in 1933.

questions.q: The Wilderness Act of 1964 was largely written by which Wilderness Society leader, who died months before it passed?
questions.explain: Zahniser wrote more than sixty drafts; the law defined wilderness as land 'untrammeled by man.'

questions.q: Which 1977 federal law required coal companies to restore land after strip mining?
options: The Resource Conservation and Recovery Act
The Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act
questions.explain: The law required companies to restore strip-mined land and created an office to oversee reclamation.

questions.q: After World War II, center-pivot irrigation on the High Plains drew heavily on which underground water source?
questions.explain: The aquifer lies beneath parts of eight states; pumping for irrigation has lowered water levels sharply in places such as western Kansas and the Texas Panhandle.

questions.q: Marjory Stoneman Douglas's 1947 book described which Florida ecosystem as a 'river of grass'?
questions.explain: The book appeared the same year President Truman dedicated Everglades National Park.
